Safety

In the high-risk world of cement plants and heavy industry, safety is not a department. It is the first principle of every task.

People and safety

  • Safety

  • Quality
  • Environment
  • Community
  • Lion country

An unforgiving workplace

A cement plant is not a forgiving place. There is height. There is heat. There are confined spaces, moving conveyors, suspended loads and live electrical systems, sometimes all within the same fifty metres.

A person can be badly hurt here in the time it takes to look away. So safety cannot be something that is added to a job. It has to be the first step of the job, every time, at every hour.

man-hours worked since 2015
2.5 million+
reportable lost-time incidents
0

This is not luck. It is discipline. What the figure means, and what it does not, is set out on Numbers, and how we count them.

The system

We operate a “Zero Harm” HSE management system aligned with international standards. Every contractor and every worker deployed under our name is held to it, and to the client’s own site rules.

Personal protective equipment
Mandatory, without exception. Helmet, safety shoes and eye protection as a minimum, and whatever else the task demands.
Daily toolbox talks
Before work begins on every shift, at the work front, in the language the crew speaks.
Medical certification for work at height
Nobody goes up who has not been examined and passed.
Permit to work
Full compliance with the client’s system. No permit, no work.
Confined-space entry
Gas test, attendant, rescue plan and a record of who is inside.
Weekly internal safety audits
Carried out by people who do not report to the job.
Site supervision
Supervisors enforce discipline from the moment a crew enters the plant gate.

Your rules are our rules

Every plant has its own safety management system, its own permit forms and its own cardinal rules. We do not bring a rival system through your gate.

Our people are inducted in your rules before they start. Where your rule and ours differ, the stricter one applies. Where your system is silent, ours fills the gap.

A day, as safety sees it

  1. Before the gate

    Fit for work. Rested, sober, in the right clothes, with the right equipment.

  2. The toolbox talk

    Ten minutes, standing, at the job. What we are doing today. What can hurt us. What we have done about it. Who is new. Any questions.

  3. The permit

    Raised for the task, issued by the plant’s authorised person, displayed at the work front. Isolations verified and locked.

  4. The work

    Under a supervisor who is watching the people and not only the progress.

  5. A change

    If the job changes, the weather changes or something unexpected is found, the work stops and the talk is held again.

  6. The end of the shift

    Area made safe. Tools counted. Permit closed or handed over. Anything unsafe that was seen is written down.

ATKAYVA

Toolbox talk record

SPECIMEN
Job
Replace gratings, packing plant, level 2
Shift and time
B shift, 14:10
Language
Gujarati and Hindi
Hazards discussed
Open floor edge. Hot work above a walkway. Dropped objects.
Controls

Permits

Specimen

The authority to stop

Anyone working under the ATKAYVA name may stop a job that looks unsafe. A helper may stop a supervisor. Nobody is punished for stopping work in good faith, even if the worry turns out to be unfounded.

This is the rule the others depend on. A permit can be wrong. A plan can miss something. The last defence is a person who sees the danger and is not afraid to say so.

When something goes wrong

An injury
First aid at once, then the plant’s medical system. The client is told immediately. Nothing is concealed, however small.
A near miss
Reported and looked into as if someone had been hurt. Near misses are free lessons.
An unsafe condition
Fixed on the spot where it can be. Barricaded and reported where it cannot.
Afterwards
We ask why, until we reach something we can change. What we learn is told to every crew, not only the one it happened to.

We count near misses and first-aid cases separately from the lost-time figure, and we show them to a client who asks.

What safety buys

Our safety record is more than a point of pride. For multinational companies a contractor’s safety history is the first page they read, and frequently the last.

But that is the lesser reason. The greater one is that every person on our sites has someone waiting at home, a few kilometres away, in a village where we will meet their family at the next wedding.

Safety first

If it looks unsafe, stop the job

અસલામત લાગે તો કામ રોકો

असुरक्षित लगे तो काम रोक दें

What each rule means

1. Permit to work
The permit is the plant’s written agreement that the job may be done, here, now, in this way. It names the hazards and the precautions. Work that is not on the permit is not done.
2. Isolation
Machines start without warning. Before a hand goes in, the energy is cut off at its source, the switch is locked, a tag says who locked it, and the start button is tried to prove it is dead. Each person at risk has their own lock.
3. Work at height
A full-body harness, hooked to something that will hold. Proper platforms and ladders. A medical certificate. Tools on lanyards.
4. Confined space
A vessel, silo, pit or duct can hold air that will not support life. Nobody enters until the air is tested, an attendant is posted at the entrance, and there is a plan to bring people out.
5. Lifting
A load can fall, swing or shift. Nobody stands or walks beneath it, ever. The area is barricaded and one person signals.
6. Hot work
A spark travels a long way and smoulders for a long time. The area is cleared, a fire watch stands by with an extinguisher, and stays after the work has finished.
7. Excavation
Under every plant run live cables. Drawings are checked, the ground is scanned and trial pits are dug by hand before a machine digs. Open pits are barricaded and have a ladder.
8. Driving
More people are killed on the road than at the work front. Seat belt. No telephone. The plant’s speed limit inside, the law’s outside. Never reverse without a signaller.
9. Machine guards
A guard is there because someone, somewhere, was once caught by that part. It stays on while the machine can move.
10. Fit for work
Gujarat is a dry state by law, and our sites are dry by rule. Nobody works under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or too tired or ill to be safe.
11. Protective equipment
The last defence, not the first. But on the day everything else fails, it is the one that is still there.
12. Stop work
The rule that covers everything the other eleven missed.

How the rules are kept

  • They are taught at induction, in the worker’s own language, and repeated at toolbox talks.
  • They are displayed at our site offices and work fronts.
  • Supervisors are judged on them before they are judged on progress.
  • A breach is never ignored. The work stops, the reason is found, and the person is retrained or, where the breach was wilful, removed from the site.
  • A supervisor who orders a breach is treated more severely than a worker who commits one.

For supervisors

No date, no client and no production loss gives you the authority to set one of these rules aside. If you are pressed to, stop the job and call the project manager. The leadership will stand behind you.

A note on language

On any one of our sites you may hear Gujarati, Kathiawadi, Hindi and several other tongues. A rule shouted in the wrong one is noise.

That is why our signs carry three languages and a picture. The Gujarati and Hindi versions of these rules are also on the pages ગુજરાતી and हिन्दी.

Heat and monsoon

For three months of the year the afternoon here will hurt a person who is not careful. For the next four the sky can empty a week’s rain in an hour. Work goes on through both, but it does not go on the same way.

3 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. The heat
  2. The monsoon
  3. Cyclones
Responsibility
  • Responsibility overview

People and safety

  • Safety
  • Life-saving rules
  • Heat and monsoon
  • Our people

Work and place

  • Quality
  • Environment
  • Community
  • Lion country

The heat

At Amreli the mean daily maximum in May is 41 °C, and the record is 46.2 °C. On a steel platform in the sun, or beside a vessel that was shut down yesterday, it is hotter than the thermometer says.

How the work changes

Hours
Heavy manual work moves to the early morning and the evening. The hottest hours are kept for lighter tasks, shaded work or rest.
Night pours
Large concrete pours begin after sunset. See Mass concrete.
Water
Cool drinking water within reach of every work front, in quantity, and people are told to drink before they are thirsty.
Salts
Oral rehydration salts or lemon water with salt and sugar, at the water point.
Shade and rest
A shaded place to sit near the work. Rest breaks that are taken, not merely permitted.
Rotation
In hot vessels and on exposed steel, crews are rotated on short turns.
New arrivals
A person new to the heat is given lighter work for the first days.
Watching each other
Workers are paired. A person in trouble with heat is often the last to know it.

Knowing the signs

AspectHeat exhaustionHeat stroke, an emergency
What you seeHeavy sweating, weakness, headache, dizziness, nausea, crampsConfusion, slurred speech, collapse or fits. Skin very hot. Sweating may have stopped.
What to doMove to shade. Loosen clothing. Cool with water and air. Small sips of water or salts. Rest. Do not send the person back to work that day.Call for medical help at once. Move to shade. Cool the body fast with water, wet cloths and fanning. Do not give drink to someone who is not fully awake.

Heat stroke kills. If a person who has been working in heat becomes confused or collapses, treat it as heat stroke until a doctor says otherwise.

The monsoon

Nearly all of the year’s rain falls between June and September, and it does not fall evenly.

How the work changes

Lightning
Work at height, crane work and work on open steel stop when lightning is near. They restart when it has passed, not when the programme would like.
Wind
Lifts of large light loads stop in high wind. Pages and scaffolds are tied.
Wet surfaces
Platforms, ladders and steel are slippery. Slower, with three points of contact.
Electricity
Every portable tool and temporary board is protected by an earth-leakage device. Cables are kept out of water. Damaged leads are thrown away.
Excavations
Pits fill and sides soften. Pumps, sumps, and an inspection of every excavation after rain before anyone enters.
Concrete
Pours are covered or postponed. Fresh concrete is protected.
Material
Cement and steel under cover. See Materials and supply.
Roads
Routes are checked before heavy loads are sent. Some roads go under.
Snakes and scorpions
The rain brings them out of their holes and into ours. Boots on, gloves on, and look before reaching into stacked material.

If someone is bitten by a snake

Keep the person still and calm. Take them to hospital at once. Do not cut the wound, suck it or tie it tight. Remember what the snake looked like if you can do so safely.

Cyclones

The Arabian Sea sends cyclones in two windows: May and June, and October and November. Most turn away. In May 2021, Tauktae did not.

When a warning is issued for this coast:

  • Crane booms are lowered and cranes secured.
  • Loose sheets, scaffold boards and light material are tied down or brought in.
  • Work at height and work near the shore stops.
  • Excavations are made safe and pumps are readied.
  • People in temporary accommodation are moved to solid buildings.
  • Vehicles are parked away from trees and hoardings.
  • We follow the instructions of the plant, the port and the district administration, and we do not argue with a signal.

After it has passed, nothing is re-energised and no structure is climbed until it has been inspected.

Who they are

A core of 130: project managers, site engineers, supervisors, millwright fitters, certified welders, electricians, riggers, masons and machine operators. The core is stable, and many have been with the firm for more than five years. Together they hold a store of knowledge that speeds up every job and prevents a good many mistakes.

Around them, a register of more than 600 tradesmen and workers, reached through local contractors and crew leaders we have known for years.

Nearly all of them are from this coast. They grew up within sight of the kiln stacks.

How they are chosen

  1. By skill

    Demonstrated in front of us. See Industrial manpower.

  2. By fitness

    A medical examination before deployment, and a further one for work at height.

  3. By character

    Background verification, and the word of people we trust.

  4. By induction

    Site hazards, the permit-to-work procedure and the code of conduct, before the first shift.

What they are owed

Wages, in full and on time
At or above the rate the law requires for the trade. Paid on the day promised, with a record the worker can read.
Statutory protection
Provident fund, state insurance and employees’ compensation cover, as the law provides.
Safe work
See Safety. Nobody is asked to do what the supervisor would not.
Water, rest and shade
See Heat and monsoon.
A decent place to stay
For those who do not go home at night: clean, with water, light and sanitation.
Respect
No abuse, no harassment, no discrimination. See Respect at work.
A way to be heard
See Worker help desk and Speak up.
No fees
Nobody pays for a job with us, or for a place on the register. See Fraud alert.

These are the standards on Labour standards, and they bind our labour contractors as they bind us.

How they grow

We invest in skill development and safety training, and we do it for a selfish reason as much as a generous one. A helper who becomes a fitter is worth more to the next shutdown. A fitter who becomes a supervisor is the person we will send to the next emergency.

The ladder from helper to supervisor is set out on Training and the ladder.

Why local

We employ local people as a matter of policy.

It makes us fast, because nobody has to travel. It makes us knowledgeable, because these people have worked inside the same plants for years. And it means that what a client pays us is spent in the villages around that client’s plant, which does more for a plant’s standing with its neighbours than any amount of public relations.

Quality that depends on a good day is not quality. Ours is built so that the right result never rests on anyone’s mood, memory or luck.

People and safety

  • Safety
  • Life-saving rules
  • Heat and monsoon
  • Our people

Work and place

  • Quality
  • Environment
  • Community

A closed loop of four controls

  1. Material verification

    Cement, aggregates and reinforcement steel are sourced from approved vendors and tested at NABL-accredited laboratories before use. A lot that fails is sent back.

  2. Process control

    Concrete mixes are designed for durability in the coastal environment, then batched, placed and cured to that design. Welding follows approved procedures. Alignment follows the maker’s tolerances.

  3. Stage-wise inspection

    Every activity requires a signed request for inspection before the next one proceeds. Nothing is buried, covered or built upon until it has been seen.

  4. Final documentation

    Test reports, inspection records and as-built drawings are compiled into a traceable quality record at handover.

The result is a paper trail that satisfies a stringent audit, because it was assembled as the work was done and not reconstructed afterwards.

The request for inspection

ATKAYVA

Request for inspection

SPECIMEN
Structure
Raw mill hopper foundation, raft
Stage offered
Reinforcement, cover, embedments and levels before concreting
Drawing
As approved, latest revision
Checked by us
Bar diameter, spacing and laps. Cover blocks at 50 mm. Bolt template surveyed. Formwork tight and clean.
Offered at
15:30, for a pour at 20:00
Client’s remark
Accepted. Two cover blocks added at the east face.
Signed
Site engineer, ATKAYVA. Engineer, client.
Specimen

Notice the remark. An inspection that never finds anything is not an inspection. We expect remarks, we act on them, and we record that we did.

What is checked, and when

Work Before During After
Concrete Materials tested. Mix approved. Reinforcement and formwork inspected. Slump. Temperature for large pours. Cubes cast. Curing recorded. Cube results at 7 and 28 days.
Excavation Services located. Levels recorded. Strata classified jointly. Founding level inspected.
Steel erection Foundation bolts surveyed. Steel checked against marks. Plumb and level. Bolt tightening. Weld inspection. Paint touch-up.
Alignment and grouting Surface prepared. Base set. Level and alignment protocol signed. Grout cubes. Final check after bolting.
Painting Surface preparation inspected. Weather checked. Thickness of each coat. Final thickness and appearance.

When something is wrong

Things go wrong on every job. What matters is what happens next.

It is reported
By whoever finds it, to the site engineer and to you. Not hidden, patched or painted over.
It is recorded
What, where, how much and why.
It is put right
To a method agreed with your engineer.
It is inspected again
And the record is closed.
It is learned from
The cause is told to other crews so that it is not repeated on the next job.

A concealed defect is a matter for vigilance, not for quality control.

Environment

This is a dry coast with salt in its soil, thorn scrub on its hills and villages beside every plant. A contractor’s footprint here is made of dust, water, waste and noise. We try to keep ours small.

3 min read

NKovaya

  2. Dust
  3. Water

  5. Spills
  6. Noise and light

People and safety

  • Safety
  • Life-saving rules
  • Heat and monsoon
  • Our people

Work and place

  • Quality
  • Environment
  • Community
  • Lion country

What we are, and are not, responsible for

The plants we work in hold their own environmental clearances and run their own environmental management. We work inside those systems and follow their rules.

What is ours is the conduct of our own work: how we dig, pour, weld, paint, haul and clean up.

Dust

For eight months there is almost no rain, and everything that moves raises dust.

At the work face
Water spray during breaking, cutting and loading.
On haul roads
Water tankers on a round.
On the highway
Every load of loose material is covered.
Stockpiles
Kept low, and dampened or covered in wind.
Housekeeping
Spillage is swept, not left to be ground into powder by the next truck.

Water

Fresh water is scarce here, and ground water near the shore is saline.

  • Curing is done by ponding, wet covers or curing compound, not by a hose left running.
  • Vehicles and mixers are washed at a designated place, not beside a drain.
  • Concrete wash-water is settled in a pit. It is not let into a stormwater drain or a field.
  • Water for concrete is tested. We do not assume a borewell is fit.

Waste

Steel scrap
Collected, counted and returned to the client or sent to an authorised dealer.
Concrete and masonry debris
Carried to the place the plant designates. Not tipped on waste land or into a creek.
Used oil, filters and oily rags
Kept apart in closed containers and handed to authorised recyclers. Never burned and never poured on the ground.
Paint tins, solvents and chemical containers
Collected and disposed of through the client’s system.
Packaging and general waste
Segregated at the site and removed daily.

A site is handed back clean. That is the fourth phase of every job. See How a job runs.

Spills

Machines carry fuel and hydraulic oil, and hoses burst.

  • Refuelling is done at a designated spot, on hard ground, with a drip tray.
  • Parked machines that leak are fixed or sent away.
  • Spill material is kept on site. A spill is contained, cleaned and reported.

Noise and light

Breakers and night work disturb people.

Where a village lies close to the work, noisy operations are kept to the day as far as the job allows. Floodlights are pointed at the work and not at houses. Drivers do not sound horns through a sleeping village.

Air

Vehicles carry valid pollution certificates and are maintained. Engines are switched off when waiting. Nothing is burned on site: not waste, not packing, not cable.

The shore and the wild

Work near the sea is governed by coastal regulations, and the client holds the permissions. We keep within the limits we are shown.

This coast is also home to the Asiatic lion, the leopard and the blue bull. We do not disturb them, feed them or leave open pits for them to fall into. See Lion country.

An honest statement

We are a contractor, and construction leaves a mark. We hold no environmental certificate and make no claim to be carbon-neutral. What we can promise is that we follow our clients’ environmental rules, that we clean up after ourselves, and that we live close enough to see the consequences if we do not.

Community

Large plants on small coasts live or die by their relationship with the villages around them. A contractor who arrives from outside with imported labour, takes the payment and leaves is a liability to that relationship. A contractor who belongs to the place is an asset to it.

2 min read

NKovaya

  3. Being a good neighbour

Responsibility

People and safety

  • Quality
  • Environment

We belong to the place

Our base is a village, not a city office. Our workforce and machinery are native to the industrial core, and not brought in from Ahmedabad or Rajkot.

Local people
We employ local youth and invest in their skills, so that a young person from this coast can build a trade here and need not leave to find one.
Local owners
Our machinery, transport and fleet partners are local owner-operators. What a client spends with us circulates through the same villages that surround the client’s plant.
Local supply
Our materials come from local supply chains wherever quality allows.
Local knowledge
We understand the social fabric of this belt because we are woven into it.

What this means for a client

The consequence is practical, not sentimental.

  • Fewer disruptions at the gate.
  • Fewer grievances.
  • A workforce that the surrounding community regards as its own.
  • A social licence to operate, which in modern project execution has become as critical as any statutory clearance.

When we promise a client a smooth operational rhythm, we are promising something we have the standing to deliver.

Being a good neighbour

A contractor is seen by a village mostly through a windscreen. So that is where good manners begin.

On the road
Our drivers slow down through villages, past schools and wherever cattle are on the road. Loads are covered. Horns are for danger.
At night
Noisy work near houses is kept to the day where the job allows.
With water and land
We do not take water from a village source or tip waste on common land.
With livestock and fields
A fence or a crop damaged by our vehicle is reported and made good.
With festivals
We know the calendar, and we plan round Navratri, Diwali, Eid and Uttarayan where the work allows. See The calendar of the coast.
With complaints
They come to us directly, and they are answered. See Feedback and complaints.

A region building its own bench

The region is training its own people. Since 2016 a polytechnic established with the Gujarat Maritime Board has been teaching diploma-level technicians at Rajula, on the doorstep of the industries that need them. Industrial training institutes across the district turn out fitters, welders and electricians every year.

We look to these young people first. See First jobs.

What we will not claim

We do not publish lists of donations, and we do not describe ordinary decency as social responsibility. Paying wages on time, hiring from the village and driving carefully through it are simply how a firm from here ought to behave.

A teacher for this page

Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj

Leadership and strategy, 1630 to 1680

He built a navy where none had been thought necessary, and raised sea forts such as Sindhudurg on rock off the Konkan coast. He moved faster than larger armies because he knew the ground. And his orders to his own soldiers were strict: take nothing from the cultivator, not even a stalk of grass, without paying for it.

What we tookWe work as guests in other people’s plants and villages. Speed and knowledge of the ground are our trade. Leaving nothing damaged behind us is our rule.

Lion country

The Asiatic lion survives in the wild nowhere on earth but Gujarat, and it has made this coast its own. Amreli district now counts more lions than any other. They cross the roads our tippers use, at the hours our night shifts drive them.

Caution

Lions cross this road at night

રાત્રે સાવજ રસ્તો ઓળંગે છે

रात में शेर सड़क पार करते हैं

Slow down after dark

અંધારું થયા પછી ધીમે ચલાવો

अँधेरा होने पर धीरे चलाएँ

Notice

Stop. Wait. Let them pass.

ઊભા રહો. રાહ જુઓ. તેમને જવા દો.

रुकें। प्रतीक्षा करें। उन्हें जाने दें।

The neighbours with the right of way

The lion walked out of the Gir forest years ago and reclaimed the scrub and the shore. Prides now live along the coast between Rajula and Jafrabad.

They cross the Pipavav–Rajula road after dark. They have been photographed walking between stacked containers at the port. Freight trains bound for Pipavav are flagged down by forest trackers so that lions may cross the line.

In the Kathiawadi spoken here the lion is savaj. People do not speak of it as a wild animal so much as a neighbour of high standing, to be given room.

It is not the only one. Leopards hunt the same scrub. The blue bull, heavy as a horse, steps on to the highway without warning and is a far commoner cause of road accidents than any predator.

How we drive

  1. Slower after dark

    On the roads of this belt at night our drivers keep well under the limit. A loaded tipper cannot stop in the distance its headlights show.

  2. Eyes on the verges

    Animals come from the side. Their eyes shine before their bodies can be seen.

  3. Stop, and wait

    If lions are on the road, the vehicle stops at a distance, dips its lights and waits. They move when they are ready.

  4. No horn, no revving, no pushing through

    An animal that is harassed is an animal that panics.

  5. Stay inside

    Nobody gets down from the vehicle. Nobody takes photographs. Nobody calls friends to come and look.

  6. Report

    A sighting on a work road is reported to the supervisor, so that the drivers behind are warned. An injured animal is reported to the forest department.

How we work

Open pits
An excavation that can trap a calf can trap a cub. Trenches and pits are barricaded, and covered or fenced when work stops. Open wells are a known danger to lions in this district, and we do not add to them.
Waste
Food waste draws dogs and cattle, and they draw predators. Site waste is removed daily.
Night sites
Lit, with people working in pairs, and nobody walking alone into scrub.
Camps
Labour accommodation is fenced and lit.
Speed inside sites
Walking pace near scrub and at the edges of a works after dark.

The law

The Asiatic lion is protected under Indian wildlife law at the highest level. Harming, chasing, baiting or teasing one is a serious offence. So is feeding one for the sake of a photograph.

We treat a breach of these rules by a driver as we would a breach of a life-saving rule.

Why it is on a contractor’s website

Because it is part of the truth of working here, and because it says something about what kind of firm one has to be on this coast.

A contractor who comes from a city sees a hazard on the road. People who were born here see a neighbour who was here first. We drive accordingly.
